background_notes.fact: Every field L satisfies the strong rank condition: an injective L-linear map L^r to L^s for finite natural r,s implies r<=s. In particular this holds for C in S001 and K in S002.

grounds.reason: V is a vector space over the standard field C; M009 is applied over C.
K is explicitly a field; M005 is applied over K.

background_notes.justification: The images of the r standard basis vectors under an injective map are linearly independent in L^s. Gaussian elimination of the s-by-r matrix uses field division by nonzero pivots and gives at most s pivot columns. Independence requires all r columns to be pivot columns, so r<=s. This verifies the strong rank premises without assuming any target dimension formula.

background_notes.fact: A finite-dimensional vector space is finitely generated as a module over its field. A finite set I of cardinality n admits a bijection Fin(n) to I.

grounds.reason: lambda is nonnegative, identifying it with ell.
The ordinary complex dimension of V is the finite integer lambda+1.
M008 makes I finite and M009 identifies its natural cardinality with n before the bijection is chosen.

background_notes.justification: Finite dimension means a finite basis exists, and that basis is a finite spanning set, which is exactly finite generation. A finite set of cardinality n can be enumerated by its n distinct elements, giving the stated bijection. Thus the chosen beta depends on an established finite cardinality, not on an unsupported choice of lattice basis.

background_notes.fact: If b:I to M is an R-basis and beta:J to I is a bijection, then j maps to b(beta(j)) is an R-basis. Over a nonzero field every vector of a basis is nonzero.

grounds.reason: H007 provides bZ as an integer basis with the corresponding complex basis.
F001 provides the finite-cardinality bijection used for beta.
qBasis is the canonical K-basis supplied by base change, indexed by Fin(n), and n=ell+1 is positive.

background_notes.justification: Under a bijection, finite coordinate families are reindexed bijectively; spanning expansions and uniqueness of coefficients are preserved. If a basis vector were zero, the finite coefficient family with coefficient 1 at its index and 0 elsewhere would represent zero, contradicting uniqueness against the all-zero family. K is a field, so 1 differs from 0.

background_notes.fact: For an algebraic tensor product over Z, a biadditive Z-balanced rule into an abelian group extends uniquely to an additive map. Two additive maps agreeing on every pure tensor agree everywhere. For a fixed scalar, equality expressing K-linearity can likewise be checked on pure tensors when both sides are additive.

grounds.reason: The tensor products are algebraic, generated additively by pure tensors with additivity and Z-balancing relations.
U uses the corresponding first-factor K-action.
The formula for F(f) is biadditive and balanced because f is Z-linear.

background_notes.justification: Present the tensor product as the free abelian group on pairs modulo the biadditivity and balancing relations. Any rule satisfying those relations descends to the quotient. Every element is a finite integer combination of generators; integer coefficients can be absorbed into a tensor factor. Additivity therefore extends equality from pure tensors to all elements. Multiplication by a fixed K scalar is additive, so equality of the two additive maps in a scalar-compatibility identity can also be tested on generators. The later applications must, and do, check their particular formulas; the background fact itself uses only the supplied algebraic tensor-product definitions.

background_notes.fact: If S:A to B is a linear isomorphism, T:A to A and Q:B to B are linear, and ST=QS, then W maps to S(W) is a bijection between T-invariant subspaces of A and Q-invariant subspaces of B, with inverse Z maps to S_inv(Z). It sends zero and whole spaces to zero and whole spaces.

grounds.reason: F004 gives the K-linear isomorphism S and its inverse.
F(f) is a K-linear operator on U.
ind(f) is a K-linear operator on V_K.
For arbitrary f0, the displayed pure-tensor calculation proves S ind(f0)=F(f0) S everywhere.

background_notes.justification: The image of a subspace under a linear map is a subspace. If T(W) is contained in W, then Q(S(W))=S(T(W)) is contained in S(W). From ST=QS and the inverse identities one obtains T S_inv=S_inv Q, proving the converse for inverse images. The mutually inverse maps S and S_inv make these subspace assignments inverse bijections. Linearity sends zero to zero and surjectivity sends A onto B.
